stances.claim: Legislative inquiries are primarily for aiding new legislation and only secondarily for recommending prosecution, so they cannot by themselves file criminal cases.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal clarification grounded in separation of powers

stances.claim: Sen. Mark Villar should inhibit and be answering questions rather than asking them, given he was DPWH Secretary from 2016 to 2021.
The Philippines does NOT need new anti-graft laws -- RA 3019, RA 6713, AMLA, and other statutes suffice; what is lacking is strict implementation.
The Philippines does NOT need a new independent commission either -- the OMB and COA already possess the constitutional mandate and powers.
Independent commissions are inherently limited because they lack contempt, subpoena, arrest, and case-filing powers, and must still refer findings to the OMB/DOJ.
The Agrava Board precedent shows independent commissions can fail to deliver justice -- decades after Ninoy's assassination, the mastermind remains unknown.

notable_anecdotes: President Marcos's now-viral 'Mahiya naman kayo' denunciation that triggered the Senate Blue Ribbon and House Infra committee inquiries.

Neophyte Rep. Leandro Legarda Leviste catching a district highways engineer red-handed trying to bribe him, filing a complaint, and triggering an in flagrante delicto entrapment -- while convincing the engineer to squeal on contractors and high officials in exchange for state-witness status.
Sen. Mark Villar's social-media-driven inhibition controversy, given his prior role as DPWH Secretary 2016-2021.

Supreme Court's stark January 8, 2013 en banc finding that 80% of court backlog involves criminal cases, paired with the September 5, 2012 observation that 40% of criminal cases are dismissed annually -- both still unimproved.

Agrava Board's enduring failure: decades after the Ninoy Aquino assassination, the mastermind remains unknown, with the convicted soldiers continuing to deny their participation despite a daylight public crime.

decision_framework_signals: Distinguish purpose-of-inquiry: aid-of-legislation first, prosecution-referral second
Apply correct evidentiary threshold to each stage: probable cause for filing, proof beyond reasonable doubt for conviction
Prefer strict implementation of existing laws over enacting new ones
Prefer empowering constitutionally established bodies (OMB, COA) over creating new commissions
Test any proposed independent commission against the contempt/subpoena/arrest/filing powers it lacks
Use historical precedent (Agrava Board) as a cautionary baseline for ad-hoc commissions
Require recusal where a legislator-investigator has prior executive responsibility over the subject agency
one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains that the Senate Blue Ribbon and House Infra committees' televised flood-control-scam inquiries -- triggered by President Marcos's viral 'Mahiya naman kayo' -- exist mainly to aid new legislation including the 2026 budget, and only secondarily to refer the criminal aspect to the OMB and DOJ for the proper preliminary investigations and the eventual filing of charges under the probable-cause standard, even as conviction will demand proof beyond reasonable doubt. He spotlights Rep. Leandro Legarda Leviste's in flagrante delicto entrapment of a district highways engineer (whom Leviste is now flipping into a state witness against contractors and higher officials) and calls out Sen. Mark Villar's conflict of interest as a former DPWH Secretary from 2016 to 2021, saying Villar should be answering questions, not asking them. His central thesis is that the Philippines does NOT need new anti-graft laws -- RA 3019, RA 6713, AMLA, and others are already on the books -- and does NOT need a new independent commission either, because the Constitution has already established the OMB and COA with the necessary powers; any ad-hoc commission lacks the powers of contempt, subpoena, arrest, and case-filing, and must still refer matters to the OMB or DOJ. He invokes the Agrava Board as a cautionary precedent -- decades after the Ninoy Aquino assassination, the mastermind remains unidentified -- and closes with a prescription against media shows and excessive talk in favor of diligent use of existing laws and institutions, speedy trials grounded in original (not photocopied) evidence, and continuous, aggressive, and patient monitoring by an incensed public.
